title: Heat and the book
teaches: Add up what every open trade loses if its stop is hit and read the total as a single percent of the account, keep that total under a cap you set, and never add to a losing trade: our size goes on at one price with one stop.

facts.quote: Placing a trade with a predetermined stop-loss point can be compared to placing a bet: The more money risked, the larger the bet.
facts.claim: Each trade with a stop is a bet, and the bet is the money you lose if the stop is hit.

facts.quote: In portfolio management, we call the distributed bet size the heat of the portfolio.
facts.claim: The bets spread across all your open positions, added together, are what Seykota and Druz call the portfolio's heat: your total open risk.

facts.quote: A diversified portfolio risking 2% on each of five instrument & has a total heat of 10%, as does a portfolio risking 5% on each of two instruments.
facts.claim: 2% on each of five positions and 5% on each of two both add up to 10% of the account at risk.

facts.quote: Setting the heat level is far and away more important than fiddling with trade timing parameters.
facts.claim: Seykota and Druz found that the level of total risk you choose matters far more than fine-tuning your entry timing.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade and allocate up to 5%–10% of their portfolio in any single position.
facts.claim: Risk per trade is set as a percent of the account, and it is a different, smaller number than the money put into the position.

facts.quote: might choose to allocate up to 5% of the portfolio in a single position, $150,000 x 5.0% = $7,500, and they might be willing to lose up to 1%, or $1,500, on a given trade.
facts.claim: In Schwab's example, up to 5% of the account goes into one position but only up to 1% is at risk on it.

facts.quote: Diversification is a simple and effective way to reduce portfolio risk, and it starts on the front end by committing only part of your capital to any one position.
facts.claim: Keeping each position to part of your capital is the first line of risk control.

facts.quote: Over time, correlations can shift, and this isn't unusual.
facts.claim: How closely investments move together changes over time.

facts.quote: The 7 deadly sins to avoid Averaging down into losing positions
facts.claim: Hirsch lists averaging down into losing positions first among the habits to avoid.

facts.quote: Over-concentration in one sector
facts.claim: Hirsch also lists over-concentration in one sector among the habits to avoid.

facts.quote: When the investor's economic and market outlook is strongly bearish (or turns negative), a more defensive posture could be instituted by limiting new buys, selling losers faster, tightening up stops and/or implementing some downside protection.
facts.claim: When the market outlook turns negative, Hirsch suggests limiting new buys and getting more defensive.

facts.quote: the risk of amplified losses that may occur from having a large portion of your holdings in a particular investment, asset class or market segment relative to your overall portfolio.
facts.claim: Concentration risk is the bigger losses you take when a large part of your money sits in one investment or one corner of the market.

facts.quote: Investments within the same industry, geographic region or security type tend to be highly correlated, meaning that what happens to one investment is likely to happen to the others.
facts.claim: Stocks in the same industry tend to move together: what hits one is likely to hit the others.

facts.quote: Or you might have investments in individual technology companies but also own a technology fund and have technology stocks represented in an index fund you own.
facts.claim: Owning companies in an industry plus a fund of that same industry doubles up the same exposure.

facts.quote: Concentration due to asset performance. Maybe one of your investments has performed very well relative to the rest of your portfolio.
facts.claim: A holding that does very well can grow into a concentration without any new buying.

facts.quote: But the stock portion of your investment portfolio won't be diversified, for example, if you only invest in only four or five individual stocks.
facts.claim: Four or five stocks is not a diversified stock portfolio.

facts.quote: You'll need at least a dozen carefully selected individual stocks to be truly diversified.
facts.claim: The SEC's guide puts real diversification at a dozen or more carefully chosen stocks.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger for a market order, not a guaranteed fill.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity when the market order executes.
facts.claim: Once a stop triggers, the fill can be far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully consider the risk of such short-term price fluctuations in deciding whether to use a stop order and in selecting the stop price for an order.
facts.claim: Pick the stop price with normal short-term swings in mind.

facts.quote: Securities with high positive correlation values move together in the same direction.
facts.claim: Highly correlated stocks move together in the same direction.

facts.quote: all with correlation values against the S&P 500 ranging from +0.87 to +0.98, the assets in your portfolio can be shown to move in very similar directions, increasing your risk exposure to singular market shocks.
facts.claim: A portfolio of names that all move alike is more exposed to a single shock.

facts.quote: The pyramid trading method simply advocates wading into a full position in small controlled chunks rather than buying 100% of your target position on the first purchase.
facts.claim: Pyramiding builds a full position in small pieces instead of buying it all at once.

facts.quote: The pyramid method allows you to buy, for example, 25% of your intended full position, set your stop and then wait for the market's next wave up to confirm the wisdom of your first purchase decision.
facts.claim: In Roze's example, the first buy is 25% of the full position, with the stop set, and the market has to confirm it before you add.

facts.quote: If it trends down, your stop is executed, you controlled your risk, and you book a small loss on only 25% of your full intended position.
facts.claim: If the first piece fails, the loss is on that 25% piece only.

facts.quote: The power of pyramid trading is that it forbids you from adding a second position unless you already show a profit on the first position.
facts.claim: You add the next piece only when the first one already shows a profit.

facts.quote: One misconception about pyramid trading is that you can pyramid down as well – this is incorrect and potentially suicidal.
facts.claim: Adding as the price falls is not pyramiding, and Roze calls it potentially suicidal.

facts.quote: they succumbed to broad market selling pressure as correlations continue to rise and the bear extends its grip.
facts.claim: In the 2022 bear market, even leading groups gave way to broad selling as correlations rose.

facts.quote: A bear market environment increases risk for all stock-related ETFs and the chance of picking winners is greatly reduced.
facts.claim: In a bear market, risk rises across stocks and the odds of picking winners fall.

facts.quote: In either case, place your stops where you think they'll work. Just adjust your position.
facts.claim: Put the stop where it belongs and change the size instead.

facts.quote: Typically, pyramiding is undertaken with a view toward concentrating resources on a winning trade, but pyramids could also be used to average or dilute the entry price on a losing trade.
facts.claim: Pyramiding usually means adding to a winning trade, though the word is sometimes used for adding to a loser.

facts.quote: Adding to a losing position is essentially a case of good money chasing after bad
facts.claim: Balsara calls adding to a losing position good money chasing after bad.

facts.quote: the effective exposure on a trade is positive and represents the maximum amount of capital at risk, assuming that prices do no gap through the stop price.
facts.claim: The money at risk to a trade's stop is the most you can lose only if price does not gap through the stop.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: Our rule: the whole position goes on at one price with one stop, and we never add to it.

facts.quote: I do not scale into trade i buy full at one spot with one stop.
facts.claim: The owner's words: he does not scale in; the full size goes on at one spot with one stop.

walkthroughs.title: Add up your stops
steps: Every open trade with a stop is a bet. The bet is what you lose if that stop is hit.
Add up the bets on all your open trades, as a percent of the account. That's your total open risk.
Ed Seykota and Dave Druz call it the heat of the portfolio. 2% on each of five trades is 10%.
So is 5% on each of two. They found that setting this level matters far more than fine-tuning your trade timing.

walkthroughs.title: Five names, one bet
steps: FINRA's warning: stocks in the same industry tend to be highly correlated. What hits one is likely to hit the others.
So five bank stocks aren't five small bets. On bad news for banks, their stops can all go the same day.
A stop is a trigger, not a promised price. If the whole group gaps down, fills can land past your stops.

walkthroughs.title: Build it in pieces
steps: No need to buy it all at once. In Gatis Roze's example, the first buy is 25% of the full size.
Set the stop. If it fails, you lose on that piece only. If it works, it has earned the next piece.
Add only after the first piece shows a profit. Averaging down is on Jeffrey Hirsch's list of seven deadly investing sins.

questions.q: What does your total open risk measure?
choices: What you lose if every stop is hit
What your worst trade could lose
Your losses so far this month
questions.answer: What you lose if every stop is hit
questions.why: What you lose if every stop is hit. Each trade's risk is the money you'd lose at its stop. Add those across every open trade and read the total as a percent of the account.
questions.lesson_line: Total open risk is every stop's loss added up, as a percent of the account.

wrong.What your worst trade could lose: That's one trade. Total open risk adds up every open trade's loss at its stop.
wrong.Your losses so far this month: Those losses are already taken. Total open risk looks forward: what the open trades can still cost.

questions.q: Your total open risk is the same as the total dollar value of your open positions.
questions.why: False. Value is the money in the stocks. Risk is what you lose if the stops are hit. Schwab's example puts up to 5% of the account in one position and is willing to lose up to 1% on it.
questions.lesson_line: Money in a trade and money at risk are two different numbers.

questions.q: Finish the sentence.
questions.sentence: Stocks in the same industry tend to move ___.
questions.why: Together. FINRA says investments in the same industry tend to be highly correlated: what happens to one is likely to happen to the others.
questions.lesson_line: Names in one industry tend to rise and fall as a group.

questions.q: Done right, how does pyramiding build a position?
choices: Buy a piece, add only as it works
Buy more each time it dips lower
Buy it all, then sell in pieces
questions.answer: Buy a piece, add only as it works
questions.why: Buy a piece, add only as it works. Roze wades in with small pieces and adds only once the first one shows a profit. Balsara says pyramiding typically adds to a winning trade.
questions.lesson_line: Start with a piece. Let the stock earn the next one.

wrong.Buy more each time it dips lower: That's averaging down. Roze calls pyramiding down incorrect and potentially suicidal, and Balsara calls adding to a loser good money chasing after bad.
wrong.Buy it all, then sell in pieces: That buys the whole position at once. Pyramiding in means a piece first, then adds as it works.

questions.q: Four open trades risk 1%, 0.5%, 1% and 0.75% of your account at their stops. What's your total open risk?
questions.lesson_line: Add every open trade's risk. That one number is what's on the line.

questions.q: The SEC's investor guide counts four or five stocks as a diversified stock portfolio.
questions.why: False. The SEC's guide says four or five stocks isn't diversified and points to at least a dozen. A short list of names is a concentrated account, so your position sizes have to carry the protection.
questions.lesson_line: A handful of stocks isn't diversified. Your position sizes have to do the protecting.

questions.q: Your account can get concentrated in one stock even if you never buy another share of it.
questions.why: True. FINRA lists concentration from performance: one holding does very well and grows into a bigger slice of the account than the rest.
questions.lesson_line: A big winner can quietly become your biggest position. Watch its size as it grows.

questions.q: Account A has four trades risking 1.5% each. Account B has three trades risking 2% each. Which has more total open risk?
questions.why: Both have 6% at risk. Four times 1.5% and three times 2% land on the same total. Seykota and Druz make the same point with 2% on five and 5% on two.
questions.lesson_line: Count the total at risk, not the number of trades.

wrong.A, it has more trades: More trades isn't more risk by itself. Each one is smaller, and the total comes out the same.
wrong.B, its trades are bigger: Bigger single trades, but fewer of them. The total comes out the same.

questions.q: A full position would risk 1% of your account. You start with a quarter of it. What do you lose if that first stop is hit?
questions.why: 0.25%. A quarter of the shares at the same stop risks a quarter of the full 1%. That's Roze's point: a failed start books a small loss on only 25% of the position.
questions.lesson_line: Start with a piece, and a failed trade costs you only a piece.

questions.q: You risk 0.5% of the account per trade. Your cap on total open risk is 5%. How many such trades fit under the cap?
questions.why: 10 trades. Divide the cap by the risk per trade: 5% over 0.5%.
questions.lesson_line: Your risk per trade and your cap decide how many names you can carry.

questions.q: Account $80,000. Four open trades would lose $600, $450, $800 and $350 at their stops. What's your total open risk?
questions.why: 2.75%. Add the four stop losses, then divide by the $80,000 account.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk over account size. Redo it after every new trade.

questions.story: Your rule caps total open risk at 6%. Your open trades risk 5% now. A new setup would risk 1.5% at your usual size.
questions.q: How do you fit it under the cap?
choices: Size it down to 1%, same stop
Same size, the cap can stretch
questions.answer: Size it down to 1%, same stop
questions.why: Size it down to 1%, same stop. The cap leaves room for 1%, so you buy fewer shares. The stop stays where you'd put it anyway.
questions.lesson_line: To fit the cap, change the size. Never squeeze the stop.

wrong.Same size, tighter stop: That squeezes the stop to fit the math. Put the stop where it works and adjust the size instead.
wrong.Same size, the cap can stretch: A cap that stretches whenever a setup looks good isn't a cap. That puts you over your own 6% limit.

questions.q: In a broad selloff, stocks from different groups can start falling together.
questions.why: True. Writing in a bear market, StockCharts' Arthur Hill showed even leading groups giving way to broad selling as correlations rose. Schwab notes correlations shift over time.
questions.lesson_line: When the whole market sells, different groups can turn into one trade.

questions.q: You hold three chip stocks and a semiconductor ETF. How many separate bets do you really have?
choices: Two: the stocks and the fund
questions.why: Close to one big bet. FINRA flags this setup: companies in an industry plus a fund of that same industry. Stocks in one industry tend to move together.
questions.lesson_line: Count bets by what moves the price, not by the number of tickers.

wrong.Four separate bets: Four tickers, one driver. If chips sell off, all four tend to fall together.
wrong.Two: the stocks and the fund: The fund holds the same kind of stocks. Wrapping them in an ETF doesn't make it a different bet.

questions.q: With a stop on every trade, your total open risk is the most you can lose overnight.
questions.why: False. A stop price is not a guaranteed fill. Once triggered, the order becomes a market order, and the price you get can be far past your stop.
questions.lesson_line: Total open risk is your plan, not a promise. A gap can cost more.

questions.story: You hold five solar stocks. Each one risks 1% of the account at its stop.
questions.q: How should you count this risk?
choices: As one bet of 5% or more
As 1%, they won't all fall at once
questions.answer: As one bet of 5% or more
questions.why: As one bet of 5% or more. Stocks in one industry tend to move together, so the stops can all go on the same news. A gap past the stops can cost more than 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Five names in one industry count as one trade. Limit the group, not just each name.

wrong.As five separate 1% bets: That's the view on paper. They share one driver, so they can all hit their stops on the same day.
wrong.As 1%, they won't all fall at once: FINRA says the opposite: in one industry, what happens to one is likely to happen to the others.

questions.story: You bought your full size at $40 with the stop at $38. It's at $38.80, under your entry but above the stop. A friend says buy more while it's cheap.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Add more and lower the stop
questions.why: Hold, add nothing. Our size went on at one price with one stop, and we never add. Buying more of a loser is averaging down, first on Hirsch's list of deadly sins.
questions.lesson_line: Never add to a losing trade. The stop decides, not the discount.

wrong.Add more, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't better here. The stock hasn't proven the idea, and adding to a loser is averaging down. We don't add at all.
wrong.Add more and lower the stop: That doubles down twice: more shares and more room to lose. The stop marks where the idea is wrong.

questions.q: If every trade risks only 0.5% of the account, you don't need to track the total.
questions.why: False. Small risks add up, and trades in one industry tend to fall together. A stop also isn't a guaranteed fill. Add up the total and keep it under a cap.
questions.lesson_line: Small per trade isn't small in total. Add it up and cap it.

questions.story: Your cap on total open risk is 6%. Five trades risk 1% each, and two of them are chip stocks. Your sixth setup is another chip stock at 1%.
questions.q: What's the problem with taking it, if any?
questions.why: Now 3% rides on chips. The total fits the 6% cap, but three of your six trades share one driver. FINRA's point: what happens to one is likely to happen to the others.
questions.lesson_line: Fitting the total cap isn't enough. Check how much rides on one group.

wrong.None, 6% is inside the cap: The total fits. The problem is that one group's news can now hit three of your six trades.
wrong.It breaks the 6% cap: Five trades at 1% plus one more at 1% is exactly 6%. It fits. The problem is the group.

questions.q: Account $50,000, cap 5% total open risk. Five trades risk $500, $400, $450, $300 and $350. How much can a sixth trade risk?

args.expr: account * cap / 100 - (a + b + c + d + e)

questions.why: $500. The cap is 5% of $50,000. Subtract what the five trades already risk, and what's left is the most the sixth can risk.
questions.lesson_line: Before a new name, find the room: the cap minus what's already at risk.

questions.story: The market is in a downtrend and your stops keep getting hit. You're at 2% total open risk with a 6% cap. A decent setup shows up.
questions.q: What's the sound move?
choices: Be picky and keep exposure low
Size up to win back the losses
questions.answer: Be picky and keep exposure low
questions.why: Be picky and keep exposure low. In a bear market the chance of picking winners drops. Fidelity's Hirsch suggests limiting new buys when the outlook turns negative.
questions.lesson_line: A cap is a ceiling, not a target. In a weak market, use less of it.

wrong.Use the room, there's 4% left: Room under the cap isn't a reason to buy. The cap is the most you'll risk, not what you should risk.
wrong.Size up to win back the losses: That's chasing losses with bigger bets, in a market where the odds of picking winners are worse.

questions.story: One position is 20% of your account, with the stop 5% under entry. That's 1% at risk. It opens 15% below your entry on news.
questions.q: About how much did it cost the account?
questions.why: About 3%. The stop turned into a market order at the open, and 15% off on 20% of the account is 3%. That's 3% against a 1% plan.
questions.lesson_line: Total open risk assumes fills at your stops. Size so a gap past them hurts but doesn't sink you.

wrong.1%, the stop caps it: A stop is a trigger, not a promised price. Below the stop at the open, you get roughly the opening price.
wrong.15%: That's what the stock lost. The account lost 15% of the 20% it had in the stock.
wrong.20%: That's the whole position. You'd lose all of it only if the stock went to zero.

conflicts: House rule check: docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 lists 'Total open risk (heat) <= 10% of the account. (App cap.)', '5 to 10 positions', progressive exposure 'pilot -> half -> full' and a 40% sector flag. None of those lines is marked as the owner's answer or quoted in his words (the 10% is credited to the app), so per the contract nothing in this unit is asked as our rule. Every cap in a question is given as 'your rule' / 'your cap'. Owner to confirm the 10% cap and pilot -> half -> full as his own if he wants them asked as ours.

Cap numbers: sources disagree on how much total open risk is sensible (search leads only: Elder's 6% rule, 6-10% on trading blogs, 20-25% on a Wealth-Lab wiki page for futures systems). None could be read on a Tier 1 or Tier 2 page (Investopedia refuses the plain client with 402 and WebFetch on 2026-11-09; the Wealth-Lab and seykota.com pages did not load), so the unit never keys a cap number as a fact.

How many names: Fidelity's Hirsch (s4, opinion) says '5-10 holdings is likely as much as one individual can effectively manage'; the SEC guide (s6) says a dozen or more stocks to be truly diversified. They answer different questions (what one person can manage vs. what counts as diversified). Only one publisher supports 5-10, so the count is not keyed; q06 keys only the SEC fact.

Scaling in: Schwab's 'How to Recover from a Big Trading Loss' suggests buying 20 shares to start, 'then adding to their position anytime the price dips', which clashes with Roze (pyramiding down is 'incorrect and potentially suicidal') and Hirsch (averaging down is a 'deadly sin'). The unit used to key add-only-on-profit, attributed to Roze; since 2026-11-09 the owner's rule A5 (sizing_rule.md section 9: 'The full size at one price with one stop; no adding'; his words in section 5: 'I do not scale into trade i buy full at one spot with one stop') rules out scaling in altogether, so w3, q04 and q09 are cut and q17 keys only 'never add to a losing trade' with our size on at one price. The Schwab page is not cited.

Measuring the risk: a position's risk can be counted from entry to stop or from today's price to the stop; the two differ once a trade has moved. Every question here uses fresh trades or states the loss 'at its stop', so the two agree. What moving a stop does to total open risk is F9.06's subject.

Word choice: the validator treats 'heat' as house shorthand, so no question, choice, why or lesson line uses it; the questions say 'total open risk'. Walk-through w1 names the term once, attributed to Seykota and Druz, because the unit title and the plan's Learn rung ('define heat') need it explained.
Seykota and Druz (s1): the page's own text reads 'risking 2% on each of five instrument & has a total heat of 10%' (a scanning typo for 'instruments'); f03 quotes it as printed.

Checker, pyramiding: Balsara (s12, f31) says pyramids 'could also be used to average or dilute the entry price on a losing trade', so the word is not used only for adding to winners, and Roze uses his pyramid on exits too (40%, 35%, 25%). q04 now asks how pyramiding works 'done right' and keys add-on-profit (Roze f26, Balsara f31 and f32 agree), so a member who knows the looser usage is not marked wrong.
Checker, Balsara (s12): the page reads 'assuming that prices do no gap through the stop price' (a typo for 'do not'); f33 quotes it as printed.

Checker, second publisher for the heat definition (2026-11-09): TD Ameritrade's 'rules to manage risk' page no longer loads (domain gone); Schwab's learn pages give only per-trade and per-position caps; everything else found was forums, indicator scripts or blogs with no named record. The definition stays on Seykota and Druz (s1) with Schwab's per-trade risk (s2). Adding the per-trade risks is arithmetic, so the keys stand.

Track audit 2026-11-09: (1) q02 and q15 are cut as duplicates of F9.02#q04 and F9.01#q16 (see verify). (2) q08's Account B now risks 2% a trade (was 3%, over the ceiling F9.01 teaches as ours). (3) A second publisher for adding up open risk exists in this track: F9.06 cites Incredible Charts' page on Alexander Elder's 6% rule (Colin Twiggs; its f42, 'Sum the risk exposure for all stocks in your portfolio'), which the second-publisher note above did not find. The 6% figure is still not keyed anywhere.

F9.02 teaches risk vs position size, so it keeps it; q01 still defines total open risk here. The question was right as written.
